questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: What life is like for people living with debt in the UK
How to get a loan to buy a house
Why British people save more than other countries
How banks decide who can borrow money
questions.why: They discuss how common debt is in the UK and hear about people on a low-income estate living with it.

questions.q: What does Neil say about saving and spending?
options: He never saves any money and spends it all
He counts every penny he spends each week
He does both, and saves mainly for his children
He only spends money on his children's needs
questions.why: Neil says he's a bit of both and tries to save, mainly because he's got children.

questions.q: What does Pippa say about the UK Citizens Advice Bureau in 2025?
options: It closed many of its offices across the country
Over 1,000 people a day contacted it about debt
It helped about 1,000 people in the whole year
It gave small loans to people who were in debt
questions.why: She says over 1,000 people contacted it every single day of 2025 for help with debt.

questions.q: Why does Jason say he has taken out loans?
options: To pay for a family holiday abroad
To start his own small building business
To buy a new car so he could get to work
The jobs available don't pay enough for a family
questions.why: He says whatever jobs there are aren't enough to provide for a family, so sometimes you need loans.

questions.q: Why does Jason mention winning the lottery?
options: To show he can see almost no realistic way out of debt
Because he recently won some money
To explain how he plans to pay his debts next year
Because he spends a lot on lottery tickets
questions.why: He says you can't see a way out, 'other than winning the lottery or something'.

questions.q: How did sociologist Ryan Davey do his research?
options: He sent long questionnaires to high-street banks
He studied government figures on household debt
He lived on a poor housing estate and talked to people
He interviewed people who work for debt charities
questions.why: Ryan spent months living on a low-income estate, talking with residents about their money worries.

questions.q: What did Ryan find about debt in Woldham?
options: Most people there had no debt at all
Only young people there were really in debt
People were far too ashamed to talk about it
Debt and late payments were a normal part of life
questions.why: He says debt was an ordinary feature of daily life, and being in arrears was too.

questions.q: What happened to Jason and his partner over the months Ryan knew them?
options: They slowly paid off all their debts together
Their money problems grew, and they lost internet
They moved to a bigger house on the estate
They both found better, well-paid jobs
questions.why: Ryan says the financial strain increased; they missed bills and their internet was disconnected.
